title: Mixed-precision robustness experiments: NaNs, accumulation, and scaling
content:
Summary:

This note records a targeted investigation into numerical instability observed in inference workloads when using mixed-precision kernels (primarily FP16) in our serving runtime. The scope includes sources of NaNs, accumulation/precision choices in GEMM and attention kernels, scaling/clamping strategies, and KV cache representations. The goal is to provide clear experimental results and actionable mitigations that can roll into runtime defaults and model onboarding checklists.

Background / motivation:

We have seen intermittent NaN failures and erratic logits on a small fraction of customer workloads during high-throughput inference (autoregressive generation, long-sequence attention). Failures typically manifest as: sudden NaNs in token logits mid-generation, extremely large logits that trigger softmax overflow, or gradual probability collapse over many autoregressive steps. These tend to correlate with models using FP16-optimized kernels, large batch sizes, and long sequence length distributions.

Hypotheses / likely root causes:

1) Accumulation precision: GEMM kernels that multiply FP16 activations and weights but accumulate in FP16 rather than FP32 can lose dynamic range and overflow/underflow for large sums (especially with long KV sequence lengths).

2) Softmax instability: NaNs/inf from exp(logits) when logits have large magnitudes. Implementation details (subtracting max, adding epsilon, not clamping) vary across kernels and can produce different failure modes.

3) LayerNorm/RMSNorm eps and fused numerics: fused kernels that perform layernorm or rmsnorm in FP16 with insufficient epsilon or fused reductions can hit divide-by-zero or catastrophic cancellation.

4) KV cache representation and incremental updates: storing keys/values in lower precision (FP16) and repeatedly reading/writing across many steps may accumulate rounding error or saturate, amplifying logits over time.

5) Quantization/dequantization scaling errors: int8-backed kernels with aggressive scaling may clip or promote out-of-range values leading to NaNs post-dequantization.

Experimental matrix (summary):

Hardware: NVIDIA A100 (40GB), H100 (80GB)
Models: small transformer (~150M), mid (~1.3B), and large (~13B) open models used internally for repros
Kernels: cuBLAS GEMM (fp16 accumulation), cuBLAS GEMM (fp32 accumulation), custom fused-attention (fp16), custom fused-attention (bf16), softmax (naive exp), softmax (stable: subtract max + clamp + eps)
Precision configs tested: full FP32, FP16 activations/weights + FP16 accumulation, FP16 activations/weights + FP32 accumulation, BF16 everywhere, mixed BF16 kernels with FP32 accumulators.
Workloads: autoregressive generation with warmup prefix lengths {0, 64, 256, 1024}, batch sizes {1, 8, 32}, token generation steps up to 2048 where feasible.

Key findings (high level):

- FP16 accumulation in GEMM produced NaNs for large sequence lengths (>=1024) and higher batch sizes on A100 for the 13B model. Switching accumulation to FP32 eliminated NaNs for the same config.

- BF16 kernels were significantly more robust than FP16 in all tested cases. BF16 rarely produced NaNs and behaved comparably to full FP32 in terms of numeric stability.

- Softmax instability was a frequent immediate cause: naive exp(logits) produced inf/NaN when logits exceeded ~88 (exp(88) ~ 1e38). Implementing the stable softmax (subtract max, clamp logits to [-60, 60], add tiny eps to denom) eliminated most softmax-origin NaNs across configs.

- LayerNorm fused kernels in FP16 sometimes produced NaN when the variance reduction fell extremely close to zero. Increasing epsilon from 1e-5 to 1e-4 or performing the variance accumulation in FP32 resolved these cases.

- KV cache stored in FP16 can be acceptable for short-lived generations, but for very long sequences or repeated context appends the rounding error accumulates and can amplify probing logits. Keeping KV in BF16 or storing keys in FP32 accumulator form reduced drift and prevented escalating logits on long runs.

- Quantized int8 kernels are fragile when using symmetric static scales that don't account for distribution tails. Using per-channel scales and median-absolute-deviation based clip thresholds reduced extreme values that would otherwise produce NaNs after dequantization in following layers.

Representative experiment (13B model, batch=8, seq=1024):

- Setup: attention implemented with a fused custom kernel using FP16 inputs and FP16 accumulation. Generation steps: warmup 256 tokens + 512 generated steps.
- Result: ~12% of runs produced NaN logits by step ~400.

Patching the fused kernel to accumulate in FP32 and switching softmax to stable version yielded 0% NaN runs in 100 repeats. Performance cost: ~5-7% throughput reduction for that kernel on A100; on H100 cost ~3-5% due to faster FP16 accumulation support.

Recommended mitigations (ranked):

1) Default accumulator precision: force FP32 accumulation for all GEMM reductions used in attention and feed-forward kernels. Rationale: large reduction lengths (seq_len * head_dim) amplify rounding, FP32 accumulation is low-cost relative to catastrophic NaNs.

2) Softmax hardening: always use stable-softmax: subtract max, clamp logits to safe range (e.g., [-60, 60]), and add eps to denominator. Provide runtime config to tune clamp thresholds per model.

3) KV cache policy: store keys/values in BF16 by default for production; for very long-context models expose toggle to store keys in FP32 (or FP32 accumulators) when seq_len > 512 or when model flagged as sensitive. Document tradeoffs in memory vs stability.

4) LayerNorm/RMSNorm: perform mean/variance accumulations in FP32 or increase eps to a conservative default (1e-4) for FP16 paths. Consider adding a fused-path that keeps interim sums in FP32 while writing output in target dtype.

5) Quantization safety: require per-channel scales for matmul inputs and a test during model onboarding that checks for post-dequantization outliers. If outlier rate > X% fall back to BF16 path.

6) Kernel-level NaN checks & graceful fallback: detect NaNs in kernel outputs (fast hardware intrinsics or a quick post-check on first batch), and if triggered, immediately fall back to a higher-precision kernel or re-run that batch with FP32 accumulators. This allows runtime self-healing without hard failures.

7) Testing and gating: add stress tests that exercise long-generation scenarios (seqs up to 2048) across precisions and hardware during onboarding. Gate optimized FP16 kernels behind these tests until stable.

Operational rollout plan:

- Short term (hotfix): enable stable-softmax and FP32 accumulators for fused-attention on dedicated-critical models and in Dedicated customer pools that reported issues. Ship as flaggable runtime config. (2 weeks)

- Medium term: update default runtime configuration: BF16 default for new kernels where hardware supports it; FP32 accumulation for reductions; KV cache BF16 default. Add per-model precision policy that can be overridden. (6-8 weeks)

- Long term: implement automatic numeric monitoring: token-level anomaly detectors (sudden entropy jumps, NaN counts), and automated canary rollouts that detect numeric regressions and halt FP16 kernel use for a model. Integrate into Redwood Console alerts. (quarterly roadmap item)

Suggested runtime flags / model metadata fields:

- numeric_precision_preference: ["auto","bf16","fp16","fp32"]
- force_accumulation_dtype: ["auto","fp32","fp16"]
- kv_cache_storage_dtype: ["auto","bf16","fp16","fp32"]
- softmax_clamp_min, softmax_clamp_max (defaults: -60, 60)
- layernorm_eps_override (default 1e-4 for fp16 paths)

Repro steps for QA team:

1) Run provided stress harness (linked in linked_artifacts) with 13B model, batch sizes {1,8,32}, seq lengths {256, 512, 1024, 2048}. Repeat 100 times and record NaN incidence.

2) Toggle the following configs and compare: a) fp16 accumulation b) fp32 accumulation c) bf16 kernels d) stable-softmax vs naive.

3) Run with KV cache stored in fp16 vs bf16 vs fp32, watch for any monotonic growth in max(abs(logits)) across steps.

Open questions / tradeoffs:

- Performance vs stability: FP32 accumulation comes with a measurable throughput cost. We need to quantify customer impact across model sizes and GPUs to decide whether automatic fallback or default FP32 is appropriate. The early experiments show H100 is more tolerant to FP16 accumulation; target heuristics might benefit from hardware detection.

- Memory budget: storing KV in FP32 may double memory for cached keys/values. For very large models and high concurrency, this is infeasible. Investigate hybrid approach: keep keys BF16 and values FP32, or keep a sparse FP32 index for recently-attended tokens.

- Quantization paths: some customers require int8 for cost reasons. We should define precise onboarding tests and safe-fallback behavior for quantized models and document expected failure modes.

Next steps / action items:

- (Jia) Produce a reproducible harness and upload to the repo (PR referenced in linked_artifacts). Include scripts for automated runs and a canonical dataset of prompts that exercise tails. (target 2024-10-22)
- (Ethan) Prototype kernel-level NaN detection and a fast FP32-accumulation fallback path. Measure perf overhead. (target 2024-11-12)
- (Maya) Add numeric checks and alerts in Console for entropy/logit anomalies and wire to canary rollouts. (target 2024-11-30)
- (Luis) Draft a model-onboarding checklist with the new numeric stress tests and precision policy fields. (target 2024-11-05)

Appendix: quick checklist for engineers debugging NaNs in inference:

- Reproduce with deterministic seed and reduced concurrency.
- Try BF16 build first; if unavailable, force FP32 accumulation.
- Inspect per-layer max/min of activations and logits to identify explosion source.
- Replace softmax with stable implementation as a quick mitigation.
- If KV drift suspected, re-run with KV cleared every N steps to see if drift stops.
- Validate quantization scales and switch to per-channel scales if high outlier rate.

Notes on terminology used in this doc:

- Accumulator: the dtype used to sum products in reduction (important in GEMM).
- KV cache: attention key/value cache used for autoregressive decoding.
- Stable-softmax: an implementation that subtracts the maximum logit, clamps range, and uses eps on denominator.

If reviewers want, I can include raw logs and the harness output (CSV) as separate files; they are currently large but will be linked into the PR. 

End of note.
